subtitle: Learn what strengths-based support looks like, how to encourage meaningful participation and which responsibilities actually apply to you when offering positive supports.
scope: For staff across DHS learning to recognize positive supports and ask useful questions within their role. The course introduces selected Minnesota positive-support requirements for providers within their actual scope. It is not required provider training, a functional behavior assessment, an individual treatment plan or instruction in restrictive or emergency interventions. Actual service, clinical, licensing, protection, access and reporting duties remain with the responsible people. Private reflection and supplied example are valid; no live records or personal disclosure are required. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Positive supports connect the person’s strengths and goals to useful skills and an environment that supports a meaningful life. They are more than a pleasant tone, and success is more than a quiet room. This course follows a practice recipe-club interest. You will distinguish observation from an explanation, examine how encouragement can carry different learned meanings, and recognize why ordinary goods and services must not become rewards that someone has to earn. You will also distinguish an everyday question from an assessment or decision that belongs to qualified and responsible roles. Learn at your own pace.

lessons.title: Connect support to a meaningful life
lessons.summary: Examine strengths and the person’s own goal rather than defining success only as compliance.
lessons.objective: Explain the strengths-based purpose of positive support strategies.
objectives: Explain the strengths-based purpose of positive support strategies.
Distinguish meaningful participation from quiet or compliant behavior alone.
Identify Dev’s stated purpose in the recipe-club fiction.
takeaways: Positive supports emphasize strengths, self-determined skills and meaningful goals.
The environment and useful alternatives matter alongside what a person does.
Selected licensing requirements have an actual scope; learning does not approve a plan.
lessons.statement: Begin with what the person wants support to make possible.

image.caption: Three people sit at a white table with laptops and notebooks; one is seated in a wheelchair.

intro.heading: Ask what the person wants to do
intro.body:
Positive supports focus on strengths, meaningful goals, useful skills and conditions that help a person live well. Minnesota’s positive support strategy definition describes an individualized, strengths-based approach that emphasizes productive, self-determined skills or alternative strategies and behaviors without restrictive interventions. A cheerful instruction or the absence of visible concern does not by itself establish such a strategy.

The rule’s purpose includes quality of life, community participation, supportive environments and goals identified by the person. Its actual licensing scope matters. Covered providers have responsibilities under the chapter and other applicable law; current license-specific requirements and exemptions also need examination. This introductory staff course does not make every learner a provider, approve a support plan or satisfy a professional qualification.

In the original learning example, Dev wants to join a neighborhood recipe club and contribute a soup recipe. Dev enjoys explaining the ingredients and wants help understanding the shared preparation steps. At the first discussion, several spoken instructions are given together. Dev stands up and moves away from the table. The account contains no injury, threat or emergency, and it does not explain why Dev moved. A draft note says “goal: stay seated and quiet.”

That draft goal does not capture the stated interest in contributing a recipe. Remaining seated might be relevant to a specific task in some circumstances, but quiet alone cannot tell you whether Dev understands, chooses to participate or has a useful way to ask for help. Examine the person’s purpose and the actual conditions before treating an outward pattern as the whole problem or imposing a restriction.

Staff within their assigned roles can ask what information, routine or assistance helps the person participate. Actual individualized planning and qualified assessment retain their requirements. Private reflection is also useful: which kinds of participation do you tend to notice, and what does your own idea of a successful group overlook? You may consider the example without sharing personal experiences or accessing a real person’s records. The aim is a clearer support question, not a classroom finding about Dev’s health, behavior or capacity.

inThisLesson: Quality of life and the environment.
lessons.keyStatement: Quiet behavior alone does not explain whether support meets the person’s goal.

flashcards.back: A strengths-based, individualized strategy emphasizing self-determined skills or alternatives without restrictive interventions.
What the person wants to do, choose, learn or experience, rather than only an organizational preference.
Conditions that help the person participate, considered alongside the person’s strengths and needed support.
The services, providers and requirements to which a rule applies, not a universal classroom authority.

accordion.heading: Read the first note more carefully

items.title: The recipe is a purpose
items.body: Dev’s wish to contribute soup gives the inquiry direction. A successful account would ask whether Dev can share the recipe and understand the preparation, not simply whether Dev stayed silent. That does not decide the full plan; it identifies why the support question matters.

items.title: Quiet is a limited observation
items.body: A quiet person could be comfortable, confused, uninterested or waiting. None of those explanations follows automatically. Similarly, moving from the table does not supply a motive or diagnosis. Keep the observed action distinct from the meaning that still needs examination.

items.title: The environment is part of the question
items.body: Several instructions were given together. That fact may help responsible people examine the situation, but it is not a proved explanation of Dev’s action. Asking about an understandable sequence leaves room for the person’s account and other relevant information rather than declaring the cause.

tabs.label: Compliance
tabs.body: “Dev remained seated” records a visible pattern if it actually occurred. It leaves the recipe, understanding and choice unanswered. Turning that pattern into the only goal could reward silence while missing the opportunity Dev wanted support to use.

tabs.label: Participation
tabs.body: “Dev shared a chosen recipe and could ask about a step” would describe a more specific opportunity and action. It still would need actual evidence and the person’s account. A meaningful goal does not let staff assume the arrangement works before it is examined.

tabs.label: Quality of life
tabs.body: “The support helps Dev pursue a valued interest” connects the activity to a wider purpose. Ask what Dev values and how the support fits, rather than deciding from an attendance count. A single club session cannot establish every aspect of a meaningful life or complete plan effectiveness.

check.question: What should the initial support inquiry preserve?
check.correct: Dev’s recipe interest, the supplied conditions and the unanswered participation question.
wrong: Only whether Dev stays seated and quiet.
A diagnosis based on moving away from the table.
A finding that the course approved a complete positive support plan.
check.feedbackCorrect: The inquiry begins with the person’s purpose and what is actually known; it does not replace assessment or approval.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Quiet alone leaves the goal and understanding unknown. Moving away does not establish a diagnosis. A course cannot approve the actual plan. Each answer replaces a useful question with a conclusion the facts or authority do not support.

items.text: Dev wants to contribute a soup recipe.
Dev wants help understanding shared preparation steps.
Several spoken instructions were given together.
Dev moved away from the table.
Moving away proves a diagnosis or motive.
A quiet room proves the support met Dev’s goal.

lessons.next: Examine what a specific observation can and cannot explain.

scenario.context: Practice work: a draft defines the support goal only as staying seated and quiet, although Dev’s stated purpose is contributing a recipe.
options: Preserve Dev’s purpose and examine the actual conditions and support needed for participation.
Approve the quiet-room goal because it is easy to count.
Diagnose the reason for moving away from the short note.
responses: This reconnects the inquiry with meaningful participation and leaves actual assessment to responsible roles.
A countable pattern does not necessarily answer the person’s goal.
The note contains an action and context, not a diagnosis or proved function.

lessons.transfer: Privately distinguish visible compliance from a purpose that support could make possible.

move.control: You keep a meaningful goal and actual information together.
move.failure: The person’s purpose disappears behind a convenient behavior label.
move.next: If useful, identify one participation question in the example. No live plan or disclosure is required.

lessons.title: Describe the observation before explaining it
lessons.summary: Keep what happened, the person’s account and a proposed explanation distinct.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a supplied observation from a motive or functional explanation.
objectives: Distinguish a supplied observation from a motive or functional explanation.
Explain the qualified-assessment boundary in the relevant rule.
Choose a more useful account of Dev’s movement from the table.
takeaways: A specific observation supports inquiry without establishing a cause.
The person’s account and relevant context matter.
Actual functional assessment belongs to qualified professionals under its applicable requirements.
lessons.statement: Describe the situation clearly without completing the explanation yourself.

image.caption: Three people sit at a white table with laptops and notebooks; one is seated in a wheelchair.

intro.heading: Keep the known action and open explanation separate
intro.body:
An observation is more useful when it identifies what occurred and the relevant context without making an unsupported judgment. “Dev stood and moved from the table after several instructions were spoken” is different from “Dev refuses to learn.” The first states the supplied sequence; the second assigns intention and closes a question that has not been answered.

The example now adds Dev’s account: “I wanted to know which step came first.” That account is important. It suggests a question about the instruction sequence without proving every reason for moving or establishing a clinical explanation. A person can also decline to describe more. Do not require a personal history before responding to an actual communication or service need.

Minnesota’s functional behavior assessment rule identifies a formal responsibility. When a qualified professional develops or modifies a written intervention to change a target behavior, the relevant assessment requirement applies. The assessment is conducted by the license holder’s qualified professional or an external qualified professional, with the applicable qualifications verified and documented. Direct observation and examination of relevant factors support a hypothesis about why the behavior occurs. A classroom note or a guessed explanation is not that process.

The rule includes biological, psychological, environmental and quality-of-life considerations through their appropriate assessments or observation. It does not authorize this learner to diagnose a health condition, demand medical records or prescribe a plan from an activity description. Actual health, safety, service or protection needs must use their responsible processes and required timing. The practice case has no emergency, and this course does not teach emergency techniques.

A useful learning account might state the instruction sequence, Dev’s movement and Dev’s own question, then identify what remains unknown. Responsible people can examine an appropriate response within the actual plan, authority and qualifications. A proposed explanation should remain a hypothesis rather than turn into a personal label. You may privately notice how quickly your own interpretation moves from action to intention. That understanding is worthwhile without a real case, a public reflection or a claim that the actual assessment requirements have been completed.

lessons.keyStatement: A sequence and a plausible explanation do not by themselves prove the cause.

flashcards.back: A specific description of an action or condition actually supplied or observed.
What the person says about the situation, distinct from what someone else assumes.
A proposed explanation to examine, not an established cause merely because it sounds plausible.
The formal assessment conducted by the required qualified professional under the applicable rule.

accordion.heading: Improve the account without inventing an explanation

items.title: Replace the intention label
items.body: “Refuses to learn” interprets Dev’s movement as a decision about learning. The known event is narrower. An account of the instructions and action lets the responsible people consider possible reasons without first having to undo an unsupported judgment.

items.title: Include the question Dev supplied
items.body: Dev’s account identifies an instruction need: which step comes first? That information can help shape the actual inquiry. It does not authorize diagnosing a processing condition or ignoring other relevant factors. Keep the account in Dev’s own stated scope.

items.title: Use the actual assessment role
items.body: A qualified assessment can involve observation and relevant biological, psychological, environmental and quality-of-life information. The process is different from a learner connecting two facts. Recognizing that boundary helps staff contribute accurate information without presenting the learning exercise as a professional conclusion.

tabs.label: Observed
tabs.body: “Dev moved from the table after several instructions” describes the supplied sequence. Its value is in its precision. It does not establish that the instructions caused the movement, that Dev intended disruption or that a particular intervention is needed.

tabs.label: Reported
tabs.body: “Dev asked which step came first” preserves the person’s own information. That question should not disappear behind a general behavior label. It can guide the relevant communication inquiry while the full explanation and actual plan remain open to appropriate review.

tabs.label: Inferred
tabs.body: “Dev moves away to control the group” assigns a function and motive the case does not provide. Even if a later qualified assessment develops a hypothesis, that would be different from proving motive through this note. A useful account identifies the open question instead of recording the guess as fact.

check.question: Which note best fits the information supplied?
check.correct: Dev moved after several spoken instructions and asked which step came first; the complete explanation and actual support response remain to be examined.
wrong: Dev refuses all learning because moving away proves intention.
The instruction sequence definitively caused every future movement.
The learner has completed the required functional behavior assessment by rewriting the note.
check.feedbackCorrect: This separates the actual sequence and account from a cause or formal conclusion not established.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The intention label goes beyond the action. One sequence cannot establish a universal cause. Rewriting a note does not meet the formal qualified-assessment requirement. Each claim closes a different unanswered question without the necessary evidence or role.

items.text: Several instructions were spoken together.
Dev asked which step came first.
What does the actual plan and responsible assessment require?
Which communication arrangement could help Dev understand the steps?
Dev intends to control everyone in the group.
The learner has proved the action’s cause from this sequence.

lessons.next: Consider how learned meanings of encouragement can change a response.

scenario.context: Practice work: a report changes “moved from the table” to “refuses to learn” without further information.
scenario.prompt: Which recommendation preserves an accurate inquiry?
options: Keep the intention label because it is shorter.
Record the specific sequence and Dev’s question, leaving explanation and actual assessment to the appropriate process.
Treat the note as authority to prescribe an intervention.
responses: The shorter label adds a motive that the account does not establish.
This gives responsible people useful information without diagnosing or completing the cause.
A classroom description does not confer assessment or prescription authority.

lessons.transfer: Privately notice where an action description becomes an intention judgment.

move.control: You distinguish observations, personal accounts and explanations.
move.failure: A plausible story is recorded as a demonstrated cause or motive.
move.next: If useful, revise the practice refusal label into a limited account. Do not enter actual clinical or personal records.

lessons.title: Understand how encouragement is received
lessons.summary: Examine different learned meanings of recognition without assuming another person wants the same response.
lessons.objective: Explain Rae’s and Nico’s different learned meanings of encouragement.
objectives: Explain Rae’s and Nico’s different learned meanings of encouragement.
Distinguish a personal account from a prediction about Dev or an identity group.
Choose an encouragement response that reflects understanding and the person’s actual preference.
takeaways: A response intended as encouragement can carry a different meaning for the recipient.
Personal accounts help widen understanding without establishing group rules.
The person’s preference matters; praise is not a substitute for usable support.
lessons.statement: Learn how recognition is understood before choosing its form.

image.caption: Three people sit at a white table with laptops and notebooks; one is seated in a wheelchair.

intro.heading: Examine recognition from more than one perspective
intro.body:
Encouragement is not understood in only one way. People can learn different expectations about recognition, visibility and relationships. Some may experience public acknowledgment as evidence that their contribution matters. Others may experience a quiet, specific acknowledgment as more respectful. These are possibilities to examine through actual accounts, not traits to assign from a person’s identity.

In the example, Rae learned in a school music group that a named public acknowledgment marked a contribution as important. A director would stop the rehearsal and tell the group what the person added. Rae learned to hear that moment as being included among the people whose effort mattered. When Dev shares an ingredient suggestion, Rae proposes announcing Dev’s success to everyone.

Nico describes a different learned experience. In a family workshop, a quiet aside about a useful contribution treated the person as a trusted participant without putting them on display. Nico learned to hear a public performance announcement about an ordinary action as distancing: the person could feel watched instead of working alongside others. Nico initially interprets Rae’s proposal as treating Dev like an exhibit; Rae initially interprets Nico’s private approach as withholding recognition.

When they explain those meanings, each has reason to reconsider the initial judgment. Rae can recognize why visibility is not always welcome; Nico can recognize that Rae intended inclusion rather than display. Understanding does not settle what Dev wants. In the supplied account, Dev says, “You can tell me quietly what helped the recipe.” That actual preference guides the response here; it does not establish that everyone with a shared identity prefers quiet acknowledgment.

A quiet, specific acknowledgment can now reflect Dev’s request while Rae and Nico retain the value of their personal insight. It cannot replace usable preparation instructions or become a reward that Dev must earn to access ordinary goods and services. Actual plans and positive-support requirements remain. You may privately consider the meaning of recognition in your own experience or use the example without disclosure. The lesson is not assigning an intercultural orientation, certifying a strategy or requiring anyone to accept personal praise.

inThisLesson: Rae’s learned meaning of visible recognition.
Nico’s learned meaning of trusted participation.
lessons.keyStatement: Understanding another account can change your response while leaving the person’s preference theirs.

flashcards.back: A response that acknowledges contribution; its meaning can depend on personal learning and context.
What an individual explains from experience, not a rule about everyone in an identity group.
Reconsidering an initial interpretation after understanding another account.
A form of acknowledgment that respects the person’s actual preference and does not replace needed support.

accordion.heading: Understand the difference rather than resolve it with a label

items.title: Visibility can express inclusion
items.body: Rae’s music-group account explains why naming someone’s effort publicly feels like welcoming them into valued participation. That explanation gives Nico information beyond a surface disagreement about volume. It does not establish that Rae’s preferred form will suit Dev.

items.title: Privacy can express equal participation
items.body: Nico’s workshop account explains why a quiet acknowledgment can preserve the feeling of working alongside others. That meaning is different from refusing to notice someone. Rae can recognize the distinction without abandoning every positive experience of public recognition.

items.title: Ask rather than complete the meaning
items.body: Dev supplies a preference for quiet, specific information. The response can follow that account without demanding a life story or assigning a cultural reason. If Dev had not answered, the preference would remain unknown; staff should not fill it from the two colleagues’ experiences.

tabs.label: Impose
tabs.body: Rae could announce the contribution despite Dev’s request because public recognition felt welcoming in Rae’s experience. That would make Rae’s meaning the person’s only option. A positive intention does not establish that the form is welcome or useful to this recipient.

tabs.label: Flatten
tabs.body: Nico could say “all praise is the same,” avoiding the different meanings to end the discussion. That agreement would leave the real distinction unexamined. Rae might continue public announcements, while Nico continues to experience them as distancing, and Dev’s request could still be missed.

tabs.label: Understand and respond
tabs.body: They can acknowledge the personal meanings, reconsider their first judgment and use Dev’s requested quiet form. The response changes because the actual accounts mattered. It is not a prediction about a population or proof that all future encouragement will be effective.

check.question: What does the exchange establish?
check.correct: Rae and Nico understand different learned meanings, and Dev’s actual preference guides the response in this situation.
wrong: Nico’s story proves all people from the same background dislike public acknowledgment.
Rae’s intention makes public praise appropriate regardless of Dev’s request.
A quiet acknowledgment settles every instruction and support need.
check.feedbackCorrect: The wider understanding makes a more responsive choice possible without erasing the person’s agency or other support questions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One account does not establish a group profile. A positive intention does not override the actual preference. Recognition cannot answer unrelated instruction needs. Each answer expands one useful piece of information into permission or proof it does not supply.

items.text: Rae describes public acknowledgment as valued inclusion.
Nico describes quiet acknowledgment as trusted participation.
Rae recognizes why public visibility may feel unwelcome.
They use Dev’s requested quiet, specific form.
Everyone with Nico’s identity wants the same acknowledgment.
One respectful exchange proves the entire support plan works.

lessons.next: Distinguish support from punishment or deprivation.

scenario.context: Practice work: Dev requests quiet information about the contribution. Rae and Nico have explained why recognition carries different meanings for them.
scenario.prompt: Which response fits the actual understanding?
options: Require Dev to accept a public announcement so the group can learn inclusion.
Treat both staff stories as rules that determine every person’s preference.
Use Dev’s requested quiet acknowledgment and retain the separate instruction-support question.
responses: An inclusion purpose does not make unwanted visibility compulsory.
Personal accounts help understanding; they do not decide another person’s preference.
This uses the actual preference while preserving other needs and the colleagues’ personal insight.

lessons.transfer: Reflect privately on a learned meaning of acknowledgment or use Rae’s and Nico’s accounts.

move.control: You understand a different meaning and respond to the actual preference.
move.failure: Your familiar form of encouragement becomes the only acceptable one.
move.next: If useful, consider which part of the exchange changed your understanding. No disclosure, assessment result or live task is required.

lessons.title: Distinguish positive support from punishment
lessons.summary: Recognize why a supportive label cannot make ordinary goods or communication things someone must earn.
lessons.objective: Explain why withholding normal goods as punishment is different from positive support.
objectives: Explain why withholding normal goods as punishment is different from positive support.
Identify the prohibited-purpose problem in the practice water proposal.
Distinguish a learning question from the actual immediate response or reporting that may apply.
takeaways: Positive support is not punishment described with pleasant words.
Normal goods and communication access must not become compliance rewards.
Actual prohibited-practice, protection and emergency requirements retain their own roles and scope.
lessons.statement: Examine what the action does, not only what it is called.

image.caption: Three people sit at a white table with laptops and notebooks; one is seated in a wheelchair.

intro.heading: Keep ordinary access outside a reward condition
intro.body:
A strategy can sound supportive while its actual effect is punitive. Minnesota’s positive-support rules identify specific prohibited purposes and actions, including punishment, staff convenience and requiring someone to earn normal goods and services. The definition of normal goods and services includes ordinary access to drinking water and other basic necessities. A friendly name or a signature on an activity sheet does not make a deprivation practice positive support.

The practice discussion now includes a proposed “encouragement routine”: Dev receives drinking water only after remaining seated and quiet through the recipe instructions. This is a proposal, not an implemented practice in the account. It connects ordinary water access to compliance as a reward condition. Staff should not introduce it as the answer to the participation question. Dev’s purpose is contributing a recipe and understanding the preparation; withholding a basic good does not become appropriate because counting quiet minutes would be convenient.

The rule also addresses withholding equipment and devices that help a person function, with a narrowly stated temporary-removal exception to prevent imminent injury or serious equipment damage. That is different from confiscating a communication aid to punish an action. The exception’s actual conditions cannot be replaced with a general concern, a course response or a convenient phrase about safety. This lesson is not permission to remove equipment or instruction in emergency interventions.

Actual restrictions, emergency procedures and related statutes have precise requirements, responsibilities and reporting. Do not treat this short course as the complete governing text, diagnose a real incident or improvise a restrictive technique. If a current safety, health, maltreatment, access or protection matter arises, use the actual required response and reporting within your role. Reflection must not delay it. Different roles have different reporting obligations; the course does not declare every learner a mandated reporter in every circumstance.

For the supplied proposal, the learning judgment is clear: do not frame earned drinking water as positive support. Keep ordinary access available and bring the actual concern to the responsible service and review roles. Appropriate positive-support inquiry can examine information, environment and useful alternatives without turning basic needs into leverage. You can practice that distinction through the example, without obtaining a real person’s records or personally adjudicating a case.

lessons.keyStatement: Calling deprivation encouragement does not change its purpose or effect.

flashcards.back: Ordinary access to basic necessities and protections identified in the rule, not things someone must earn through compliance.
A condition intended to punish an action or compel compliance by withholding something otherwise available.
A limited provision with its own actual conditions; it is not permission created by a broad safety label.
The required protection, service, health or reporting process in the real role and circumstances.

items.title: The water remains a normal good
items.body: The proposal does not turn water into a special optional bonus. It makes ordinary access contingent on the desired behavior. A reassuring title cannot remove that dependency or make the proposal consistent with the person’s self-determined participation goal.

items.title: A signature cannot fix the wrong authority
items.body: A signed activity sheet would not automatically establish an exception or approve punishment. Actual governing scope, requirements and responsible decisions remain. Do not use the exercise to make a real rights modification or introduce a restrictive procedure.

items.title: Respond to a present concern through the actual process
items.body: A proposed practice can require an appropriate responsible review before anything is introduced. If there is an actual current harm, deprivation or other reportable concern, use the response that applies to your role and the circumstances. It must not wait for the next lesson or a private reflection.

tabs.heading: Compare support, leverage and an exception

tabs.label: Support
tabs.body: An understandable sequence and a usable way to ask about a step address participation. Their fit still needs actual assessment and planning as applicable. They differ from using water as leverage because they aim to make a meaningful opportunity usable rather than withhold an ordinary good for compliance.

tabs.label: Leverage
tabs.body: “Remain quiet to receive water” turns an ordinary need into a condition for the staff-preferred action. A smile or an encouragement label does not change that effect. The rule’s prohibited-purpose boundaries matter more than whether the proposal sounds calm.

tabs.label: Exception
tabs.body: An actual narrow equipment-protection exception has specified conditions, not a general promise that staff may remove anything inconvenient. Applying it needs the actual facts and requirements. This example contains no emergency and supplies no authority for an equipment restriction or technique.

check.question: How should the proposed earned-water routine be understood?
check.correct: It makes a normal good contingent on compliance and must not be introduced as positive support; use the actual responsible response for any current concern.
wrong: It becomes positive support if staff use a friendly title.
It is authorized whenever a signed activity sheet mentions it.
It should be tried first, with any protection response delayed until the course ends.
check.feedbackCorrect: The actual condition, not its label, reveals the deprivation problem. Required responses cannot wait for a course.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A pleasant title does not alter withholding. A signature does not establish a lawful exception or authorization. Trying it first could expose someone to the practice and delay the actual response. Each shortcut avoids the substantive boundary instead of examining it.

items.text: Ask how Dev can understand and ask about a preparation step.
Examine an appropriate routine through the actual plan and roles.
Ordinary drinking water must not be a punishment or compliance reward.
Current protection and reporting responsibilities cannot wait for reflection.
A friendly title permits withholding normal goods.
A broad safety phrase authorizes any equipment removal.

lessons.next: Connect support questions to actual planning and assessment roles.

scenario.context: Practice work: a draft proposes water only after Dev stays quiet and asks the learner to approve it as encouragement.
options: Do not introduce the condition as positive support; preserve ordinary access and use the actual responsible response and review.
Approve it because the word punishment is absent.
Run the experiment before deciding whether any actual protection responsibility applies.
responses: This recognizes the actual deprivation effect and preserves responsible procedures without inventing an authorization.
The effect does not depend on the chosen label.
Experimentation must not delay a required response or introduce a prohibited practice.

lessons.transfer: Privately examine what a proposed action does rather than relying on its title.

move.control: You recognize a normal-access condition and preserve actual response responsibilities.
move.failure: A pleasant label or signature is treated as permission for punishment.
move.next: If useful, explain the water proposal’s problem using the example. Do not practice a restrictive technique or enter a real incident.

lessons.title: Connect the support question to the actual plan and roles
lessons.summary: Distinguish an everyday inquiry from the responsibilities for an individualized strategy and qualified assessment.
lessons.objective: Explain the actual license-holder planning and evaluation responsibilities discussed in the rule.
objectives: Explain the actual license-holder planning and evaluation responsibilities discussed in the rule.
Distinguish a suggested communication arrangement from an approved individualized strategy.
Choose a useful next account within the learner’s actual role.
takeaways: A strategy requires individual strengths, needs and preferences, not a copied routine alone.
Actual plan, professional qualification and evaluation responsibilities retain their scope.
A present need does not have to wait for a course or a routine review date.
lessons.statement: Contribute useful information without substituting for the responsible process.

image.caption: Three people sit at a white table with laptops and notebooks; one is seated in a wheelchair.

intro.heading: Keep the proposal and the formal responsibility distinct
intro.body:
Positive-support inquiry can produce useful suggestions, such as making an instruction sequence understandable or providing a way to ask about a step. Suggestions are not automatically approved strategies. For license holders governed by the relevant rule, positive support strategies must be incorporated in writing into the existing required individual plan. They need to reflect assessed strengths, needs and preferences and the actual strategy standards, including evidence, ethics, person-centeredness, least restriction and effectiveness.

The rule also places evaluation responsibilities on the covered license holder. At least every six months, the license holder evaluates with the person whether the strategies meet the standards and whether the services support individual preferences, daily needs and goals, then makes appropriate changes when needed. That is an actual scoped responsibility, not a new six-month deadline for every DHS learner’s reflection. It does not mean staff should leave a current need or concern unanswered until a scheduled evaluation.

In the example, the useful question is whether a short sequence and a way to ask “which step first?” could help Dev pursue the recipe interest. The learner can retain Dev’s account and identify that question. Actual responsible service and planning roles need to examine what the plan requires and whether the proposed arrangement fits. If the situation involves developing or modifying a written intervention to change a target behavior, the qualified-assessment requirement discussed earlier remains. A course response does not become that assessment by using professional-sounding words.

Requirements vary with actual license type, program and governing law. DHS’s current training announcement distinguishes license-specific resources and statutory exemptions. This course is an introduction for staff, not the complete required provider preparation or a license qualification. Avoid claiming that every setting has identical duties or that finishing a lesson authorizes independent clinical or behavioral work.

A useful account names Dev’s purpose, the supplied instruction question and the proposed arrangement, with its approval status clear. It does not require forwarding a complete personal or medical file to every participant. Actual information handling and responsible response requirements apply. Staff can ask a better question and use the appropriate process without taking over another role. You can also keep the reflection private and use the example. Both support meaningful understanding; neither certifies that an actual individual plan or provider evaluation meets every requirement.

lessons.keyStatement: A helpful proposal is information for the responsible process, not a completed assessment or authorization.

flashcards.back: A strategy grounded in the person’s assessed strengths, needs, preferences and actual requirements.
The required individual plan into which the covered license holder incorporates the strategy.
The actual scoped review of fit and standards, rather than a staff-only assumption that a routine works.
The actual professional or provider requirements, not authority gained by finishing this course.

accordion.heading: Prepare a useful question for the responsible process

items.title: Explain the purpose and condition
items.body: An account saying only “change Dev’s behavior” loses the recipe goal and instruction question. Naming the actual interest and supplied account gives responsible people information relevant to support. It does not decide whether a particular formal intervention is needed.

items.title: Identify the proposal’s status
items.body: A short instruction sequence can be a proposal to examine rather than an arrangement already approved. Keeping that status visible prevents the learning note from appearing to change an actual plan. Responsible people need to apply the relevant requirements and roles, not merely adopt the learner’s preferred wording.

items.title: Do not wait out a current need
items.body: The periodic evaluation requirement is not permission to postpone a present health, safety, access or service concern. Use the process and response required for the actual need. A lesson or scheduled discussion must not become a gate to ordinary assistance or required reporting.

tabs.label: Contribution
tabs.body: The learner can preserve Dev’s account and name the open instruction question. That contribution may improve what responsible people understand. It does not require a diagnosis or complete personal file, and it does not authorize the learner to implement every suggested change.

tabs.label: Assessment
tabs.body: The relevant qualified professional conducts the formal functional assessment when its rule conditions apply. Direct observation and appropriate factors support a hypothesis. The process needs actual qualifications and information; a convincing classroom explanation or rewritten label cannot replace it.

tabs.label: Evaluation
tabs.body: The covered license holder evaluates the strategy and person-centered services with the person under the actual requirements. A meeting held or a form signed is not by itself evidence of effectiveness. The evaluation needs to examine fit and standards and lead to appropriate changes where needed.

check.question: Which account supports the actual planning work?
check.correct: Dev wants to contribute a recipe and asked about the first step; the proposed communication arrangement needs examination through the actual plan and responsible roles.
wrong: The learner approved the strategy by completing this exercise.
Copy the same routine into every person’s plan without examining preferences.
Delay a current access or safety concern until the routine six-month review.
check.feedbackCorrect: This contributes specific information while retaining individualization, authority and the response required for current needs.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Course completion is not approval authority. A copied routine omits the individual inquiry and actual standards. A periodic evaluation does not authorize delaying a present required response. Each shortcut changes a responsibility rather than completing it.

items.text: Preserve Dev’s stated recipe interest and instruction question.
Identify the proposal as unconfirmed rather than implemented.
Apply the actual qualified-assessment requirement when its conditions are met.
Evaluate with the person under the covered license-holder requirements.
Course completion authorizes a clinical intervention.
Every current concern may wait for a periodic review.

scenario.context: Practice work: a learner drafts a clearer instruction proposal and is asked to record the individual strategy as approved. No responsible review or decision is supplied.
scenario.prompt: Which response preserves the actual roles?
options: Record approval because the proposal sounds person-centered.
Identify it as a proposal, retain Dev’s purpose and question, and use the actual plan and qualified roles as required.
Require Dev to finish the course before the proposal can be considered.
responses: A useful idea does not supply the missing decision or requirements.
This gives responsible people useful information without inventing approval or qualification.
Learning is not a prerequisite for the person’s actual support process.

lessons.transfer: Privately distinguish an information contribution from the decision it can help inform.

move.control: You preserve the specific question, actual plan and responsible authority.
move.failure: A course proposal or copied routine is treated as a complete individual strategy.
move.next: If useful, describe the proposal’s status in the example. Do not modify an actual plan through this exercise.

lessons.title: Read support results in relation to the person’s goal
lessons.summary: Distinguish an observed session, the person’s account and wider effectiveness claims.
lessons.objective: Distinguish Dev’s stated experience from a proved explanation or lasting outcome.
objectives: Distinguish Dev’s stated experience from a proved explanation or lasting outcome.
Identify the unanswered question in the final practice account.
Choose a summary that preserves meaningful participation and actual evaluation responsibilities.
takeaways: A useful result answers a particular question without proving every broader outcome.
The person’s account matters alongside observation and the actual plan.
Missing feedback and mixed experience remain information to examine, not success or failure by default.
lessons.statement: Say what the support helped make possible and what remains unknown.

intro.heading: Keep meaningful participation visible in the result
intro.body:
Positive supports aim to help a person pursue meaningful goals and useful skills in a supportive environment. Reading results only through quietness can miss that purpose. At the same time, a favorable story cannot establish every requirement or demonstrate lasting effectiveness. Distinguish what was offered, what occurred, what the person said and what remains unanswered.

The final practice account supplies three club sessions after an instruction arrangement was established through the responsible process. In two sessions, Dev used a short step sequence, asked about the first step and contributed ingredients to the soup discussion. Dev said that the sequence helped explain what to do next. In the third session, the information about the instruction arrangement and Dev’s experience is missing. No broader qualified assessment or long-term result is supplied by this account.

The two accounts can support a limited statement about useful participation and Dev’s reported understanding. They cannot prove that the sequence caused every action, that all concerns disappeared or that the same arrangement will suit everyone. The third session remains unknown. Calling it successful because no concern was recorded would invent reassurance; calling it failed because no account was recorded would make the opposite unsupported judgment.

The actual covered license holder’s evaluation with the person and other applicable plan, qualified-assessment and reporting requirements remain. A classroom summary is not the complete evaluation. Responsible people may need further information about fit, meaningful goals, support and continued needs. If a current matter requires a response, missing learning feedback does not allow the response to wait. Do not use a satisfaction statement to waive standards or a behavior count to infer personal worth.

Rae and Nico can also retain their private understanding of recognition and encouragement. That personal learning has value without public disclosure, an employee score or a demanded work product. It is distinct from Dev’s experience and the provider’s formal responsibilities. You may use the example to practice a truthful account or simply reflect on the difference between a limited result and a sweeping claim. Progress can be specific and incomplete without needing a story of universal success.

Dev’s account and the two sessions.
lessons.keyStatement: A limited useful account is meaningful without being proof of universal effectiveness.

flashcards.back: What the person says about a particular arrangement, within the scope of the actual account.
An unanswered item that establishes neither success nor failure on its own.
Examination of how the actual support fits meaningful goals and applicable standards, not only a quiet period.
Personal understanding that need not be disclosed or converted into an individual score.

items.title: Keep the participation result visible
items.body: Dev asked about a step and contributed ingredients in the supplied two sessions. That account is more specific than “behavior improved.” It connects the arrangement to the recipe goal while leaving the cause and longer-term fit open to actual assessment and evaluation.

items.title: Keep the missing session unknown
items.body: No instruction or experience account is supplied for the third session. The absence of a recorded concern is not evidence that everything worked; the absence of a success story is not proof of failure. A truthful summary names the gap rather than borrowing reassurance or a negative label.

items.title: Keep personal and formal learning distinct
items.body: Rae and Nico’s perspective change is their own learning; Dev’s account concerns the club experience; the covered license holder has actual evaluation duties. None of those can stand in for all the others. Preserving the distinctions makes each contribution clearer without a compulsory public proof of growth.

tabs.heading: Compare a report, a cause and a wider claim

tabs.label: Report
tabs.body: “Dev said the sequence helped explain the next step” preserves the actual personal account. It can inform responsible review alongside other relevant facts. It does not mean every possible support need was identified, every standard met or the person approved every future arrangement.

tabs.label: Cause
tabs.body: “The sequence caused all participation changes” reaches beyond the two accounts. Other conditions and the actual assessment may matter, and the third session is unknown. A plausible explanation can guide an inquiry without becoming demonstrated causality in this classroom summary.

tabs.label: Wider claim
tabs.body: “Positive supports now work for everyone at the club” generalizes from limited fiction to people and situations not examined. The useful result belongs to its actual scope. Keep the next unanswered question and responsible evaluation visible rather than expanding a favorable report into a guarantee.

check.question: Which summary fits the final practice account?
check.correct: The two supplied sessions include useful participation and Dev’s reported understanding, while the third session and broader effectiveness remain unknown.
wrong: The missing session proves there were no concerns.
The two sessions establish the arrangement’s cause and success for everyone.
No useful result can be described until every long-term outcome is known.
check.feedbackCorrect: This acknowledges meaningful evidence without expanding it into a cause, a universal claim or a complete evaluation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Missing information cannot establish reassurance. Two limited accounts cannot demonstrate universal effectiveness or causality. Unanswered broader questions do not erase the supplied useful participation. Each answer either inflates or dismisses the actual evidence.

items.text: Dev contributed ingredients in the two described sessions.
Dev said the short sequence helped explain the next step.
The third session’s instruction arrangement and experience are unknown.
The actual responsible evaluation must examine continued fit and requirements.
No recorded concern proves the missing session succeeded.
One useful arrangement must work for every person.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to connect meaningful goals, accurate inquiry and actual responsibilities.

scenario.context: Practice work: a report says three sessions prove the strategy works universally. Only two sessions and Dev’s limited account are described.
options: Keep the universal claim because positive language encourages staff.
Remove every useful result because one session lacks information.
Describe the two supplied accounts, keep the missing session unknown and retain the actual evaluation responsibilities.
responses: Encouragement cannot establish the missing facts or a universal outcome.
A gap limits the conclusion but does not erase the useful information supplied.
This connects the result to its evidence and purpose without deciding the unknown or replacing formal duties.

lessons.transfer: Privately distinguish a useful limited result from a wider claim it cannot establish.

move.control: You describe meaningful participation and the limits of the account.
move.failure: Quietness, missing feedback or a favorable story is treated as complete effectiveness.
move.next: If useful, summarize the example or keep a reflection private. No real file, clinical conclusion or public learning proof is required.

jobAid.title: Ask what the support helps the person do
jobAid.subtitle: Keep strengths, meaningful goals, observed conditions and actual responsibilities together.
jobAid.intro: Use the recipe-club an example or reflect privately. This aid is not an individual assessment, intervention plan, approval or substitute for an actual required response.

sections.heading: Begin with a meaningful goal
items: Ask what the person wants to do, choose, learn or experience, rather than defining success only as quiet behavior.
Distinguish supplied observations and the person’s actual account from inferred motives, functions or diagnoses.
Consider usable communication, an understandable routine and appropriate support within the actual plan and role.

sections.heading: Respect choice and formal boundaries
items: Learn how encouragement is understood by this person; do not predict a preference from identity or impose public praise.
Do not make normal goods, services or communication devices things a person must earn through compliance. Applicable prohibition and exception requirements retain their exact scope.
Use actual qualified assessment and responsible service/licensing roles. Learning does not authorize a strategy, restraint, service change or rights modification.

sections.heading: Read the result honestly
items: Describe the opportunity and support actually provided, the person’s account and what remains unknown.
A quiet period or one useful session does not establish lasting effectiveness, the behavior’s cause or complete compliance.
Current safety, health, service or protection needs retain their required response and reporting. Do not delay them for a learning exercise.

remember: Positive supports concern meaningful quality of life as well as useful skills and alternatives.
An observation is not a diagnosis or a demonstrated explanation.
A supportive label cannot turn punishment or deprivation into positive support.
Private personal understanding and supplied practice do not require a live work product.
Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
